title: Coral Reefs
keyIdea: Coral is not rock and not a plant. It is made by tiny soft animals called polyps, cousins of jellyfish, that catch plankton with their tentacles. Each polyp builds a hard limestone cup. When it dies the cup stays, and new polyps grow on top, so a reef grows slowly over thousands of years and only its top layer is alive. Tiny algae living inside the polyps use sunlight to make food, so reef corals need warm, clear, shallow water. Water that is too hot makes them push out their algae and turn white (bleaching). A reef's caves, cracks and branches give homes to a huge variety of animals: reefs cover less than 1% of the sea floor but hold about a quarter of all sea species, so they are called the rainforests of the sea.
familyTip: Look at a photo or video of a coral reef together. Count how many different kinds of animals you can spot, and talk about where each one is hiding or feeding.

visual.caption: Is it true about coral? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then a box.

items: Coral is made by tiny animals
Only the top layer of a reef is alive
Coral is a kind of rock
Coral grows best in deep, dark water

lab.caption: Flagship lab: open coral polyps, grow a reef 100 years a tap, find where coral grows best, house six reef animals, see why reefs are sea rainforests.

kid: Coral looks like rock, and some coral looks like a plant. But coral is made by animals! Each tiny bump on a coral branch is a polyp. A polyp is a small soft animal with a ring of tentacles. It is a cousin of the jellyfish. At night it opens its tentacles to catch tiny drifting food called plankton.

Each polyp builds a hard cup of limestone under its soft body. When a polyp dies, its cup stays. New polyps grow on top. Layer after layer, the cups pile up into a reef. This is very slow. Many reefs grow about a centimetre a year, so a big reef takes thousands of years. Only the thin top layer is alive.

Tiny algae live inside each polyp. Like plants, they use sunlight to make food, and they share it with the polyp. So reef coral needs warm, clear, shallow water where light reaches. If the sea gets too hot, the polyps push the algae out and turn white. This is called bleaching. If the heat lasts, the coral can die.

A reef is full of caves, cracks, ledges and branches. Fish, crabs, octopuses, eels and turtles all find places to hide and food to eat. Reefs cover a tiny part of the sea floor, but about a quarter of all sea creatures live there. That is why people call them the rainforests of the sea.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This supports the National Curriculum in England for Year 4 (living things and their habitats; recognise that environments can change and this can sometimes pose dangers to living things) and Year 2 habitats, and NGSS 3-LS4-3 (some organisms survive well in a habitat, some less well, some not at all). Facts are from NOAA's Coral Reef Conservation Program: polyps are cnidarians that secrete calcium carbonate skeletons, reef-building corals host zooxanthellae algae, and reefs cover under 1% of the ocean floor while supporting about 25% of marine species.

The lab has five tasks. Learners open polyps on a coral branch, grow a reef 100 years per tap until it reaches sunny water, and drag a coral to five places to find that only warm, clear, shallow water works; very hot water shows bleaching. Then they give six animals the part of the reef each one uses, and pick the three true reasons for the rainforest name.

Common mistakes. Many children think coral is a rock or a plant, because it is hard and branched and does not seem to move. They also think the whole reef is alive, or that white coral is clean and healthy. Some think coral can live anywhere in the sea. Ask: what would happen to the algae in deep, dark water? Be careful with the word 'algae': the algae are the plant-like partner, the polyp is the animal.

choices: A tiny soft animal with tentacles
practice.hint: Think about what the bumps did when you opened them in the lab.
practice.explain: A polyp is a tiny animal, a cousin of the jellyfish. It catches plankton with its tentacles and builds a limestone cup.

practice.prompt: A reef grows about 1 centimetre a year. About how many years does it take to grow {n} metres? (1 metre = 100 centimetres)
practice.hint: Each metre is 100 centimetres, and it grows 1 centimetre a year.
practice.explain: {n} metres = {=100*n} centimetres. At 1 centimetre a year that takes about {=100*n} years.

practice.prompt: Why do reef corals need clear, sunny water?
choices: Algae inside the polyps use sunlight to make food
Polyps need light to see their food
practice.explain: The algae inside the polyps make food from sunlight and share it. In dark or muddy water they cannot, so the coral starves.

practice.prompt: A coral branch has {n} rows of polyps with {m} polyps in each row. How many polyps is that?
practice.hint: Rows times polyps in each row.
practice.explain: {n} rows × {m} polyps = {=n*m} polyps. Every one is a separate tiny animal.

practice.prompt: Part of a reef has turned white after the sea got too hot. What has happened?
choices: The polyps pushed out their algae: bleaching
The coral is clean and healthy
practice.explain: Heat stress makes polyps push out their algae, so the coral turns white. Without the algae's food it can die if the heat lasts.

pool.prompt: Which part of a big reef is alive?
choices: The thin layer of polyps on top
All of it, right to the bottom
pool.hint: What is left when a polyp dies?
pool.explain: Living polyps are only on the top. Underneath are limestone cups left by polyps that died long ago.

pool.prompt: Where would reef coral grow best?
pool.explain: Warm, clear, shallow water lets sunlight reach the algae. Dark, cold or muddy water stops the coral from getting food.

pool.prompt: Why are coral reefs called the rainforests of the sea?
choices: They are home to a huge variety of living things
It rains on them a lot
pool.hint: What do rainforests have a lot of?
pool.explain: Like rainforests, reefs pack a huge variety of life into a small area with many layers and hiding places.

pool.prompt: How does a coral polyp catch its food?
pool.hint: Think of its cousin, the jellyfish, and its stinging arms.
pool.explain: Polyps open their tentacles, often at night, and catch tiny drifting plankton. They also get food from their algae.

pool.prompt: A diver counts {n} kinds of fish on a reef and {m} kinds on the bare sand next to it. How many more kinds are on the reef?
pool.hint: Take the sand count away from the reef count.
pool.explain: {n} − {m} = {=n-m} more kinds on the reef. Its caves and cracks give many more places to live.

pool.prompt: Why is a reef full of caves, cracks and ledges good for animals?
choices: They give places to hide, rest and find food
pool.hint: What do small fish need to stay safe?
pool.explain: Each nook is a hiding place or a feeding place, so many different animals can live close together.

pool.prompt: A reef grew 1 centimetre each year for {n} years. How many centimetres did it grow?
pool.explain: 1 centimetre × {n} years = {=n} centimetres. Reefs grow slowly.

pool.prompt: Sam says coral is a plant because it does not walk about. What is the best answer?
choices: Coral is made of animals that stay in one place and catch food
Sam is right: things that stay still are plants
Coral is a rock, not a plant
pool.explain: Polyps stay fixed to their cups, but they are animals: they catch and eat food with tentacles. The algae inside are the plant-like part.

pool.prompt: What do the tiny algae inside polyps give the coral?
choices: Food made from sunlight, and colour
pool.hint: What do plant-like things make with sunlight?
pool.explain: The algae make food from sunlight and share it, and they give coral its colours. The polyp itself builds the limestone cup.
